findings.title: RSA key generation
findings.remediation: It isn't clear from this line whether the key encrypts or signs. If it encrypts or does key exchange, treat it as urgent (hybrid ML-KEM); if it signs, it can wait for ML-DSA. Also note where the key is stored and how long the data it protects needs to stay secret.

findings.title: RSA encryption (OAEP / PKCS#1 v1.5)
findings.remediation: Anything encrypted this way can be recorded now and decrypted later, once a quantum computer exists. Switch key exchange to a hybrid of X25519 and ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203). In TLS that means enabling the X25519MLKEM768 group, which OpenSSL 3.5+ and Go 1.24+ support. If the app wraps data keys with RSA-OAEP or ECDH itself, use a hybrid KEM there instead.

findings.title: SSH public key
findings.detail: ssh-rsa, 1024 bits; classically weak (DSA or RSA < 2048)
findings.remediation: A quantum computer could forge these signatures, but it can't go back and break old ones, so this can usually wait until key exchange is done. The replacement is ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204), or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for long-lived roots and firmware signing. Reading the algorithm from config makes the switch much easier later.

plan.title: Wave 1: key exchange and encryption
plan.why: Data encrypted with RSA or ECDH today can be stored and decrypted later, so this goes first. The usual fix is hybrid ML-KEM.

plan.why: To forge a signature you need the quantum computer at the time of the attack, so this can come after key exchange. Start with the long-lived stuff: root certificates, firmware and code signing.
